analysis.one_liner: Requires websites to get parental consent before collecting kids' personal data and orders agencies to study adult online privacy.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in a House subcommittee when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999; Congress enacted a near-identical children's online privacy law weeks after it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for commercial websites to collect personal information from young children without clear notice to parents, verifiable parental consent, and parents' ability to review and block further use of their child's data, with the Federal Trade Commission enforcing violations. It would also have let websites avoid the rules by following industry-written guidelines approved by the FTC. For adults, it would not have created any new privacy rights; it would have directed the FTC and FCC to study the problem and report back to Congress with recommendations. The bill was introduced in the final month of the 105th Congress, referred to the House Commerce Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never acted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and children under 13, who would gain notice, consent, and access rights over personal information collected by children's websites; FTC-verified industry self-regulation groups; consumers generally would get only study papers, not rules.

how_it_helps.text: Children's websites would have to clearly disclose their data practices, obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from a child under 13, and give parents access to the data plus the right to refuse further use or collection [S2][S3].
Violations would be treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act, enforceable by the FTC with its usual penalty powers [S2][S3].
Website operators would have to keep reasonable procedures to protect the confidentiality, security, accuracy, and integrity of personal information collected from children [S3].

The FTC and FCC would have been required to run proceedings on whether consumers can know when data is collected about them online and can stop its unauthorized use, reuse, disclosure, or sale, and recommend legislative fixes [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial website operators and online services, which would face notice, parental-consent, data-security, and compliance costs for children-directed sites; any future adult privacy rules were deferred to study, not imposed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Commercial website and online service operators

drawbacks.text: The bill is internally inconsistent: it defines a 'child' as anyone under 16 [S3], but its core prohibition and consent requirements apply only to collecting information from children under 13 [S2][S3], leaving ambiguous what protection older teens would get.

Its safe-harbor provisions would deem operators compliant if they follow guidelines written by computer industry representatives and approved by the FTC [S2][S3], putting the industry largely in charge of writing the rules it would live under.
Adults would get no new privacy rights under this bill, only agency studies and reports to Congress due within a year of enactment [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For its main purpose, the bill was a reasonable, enforceable design: notice, verifiable parental consent, and parental access are the core tools later used in federal children's privacy law, and the FTC enforcement hook gives them teeth. Its weaknesses are real but bounded: it protects only young children (and its under-13/under-16 definitions conflict), it outsources compliance to industry-written guidelines, and it does nothing for adult privacy beyond ordering studies. On balance a consumer-protection bill with modest costs to website operators and few direct benefits for adults.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the last month of the Congress, it was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection Subcommittee, and it died there without ever getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey (D-MA) introduced the Electronic Privacy Bill of Rights Act of 1998 in the House on October 1, 1998 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Commerce on October 1, 1998, and on October 5 to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection [S5].
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, commercial website operators faced no new federal obligations from this bill. That loss was largely symbolic in practice: weeks after this bill was introduced, Congress enacted a closely similar children's online privacy law (the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, which Markey also sponsored) in October 1998, so the children's privacy rules did become law by a different route, while the bill's adult-privacy proposals produced nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Website operators, though similar children's privacy rules passed anyway

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].

against.name: Rep. Tom Bliley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for committee action; after referral to the Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection Subcommittee on October 5, 1998, the committee took no action on it [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and only one Democrat sponsored the bill with zero cosponsors, so no partisan pattern can be measured.

industries.industry: Commercial website and online service operators
industries.note: Children-directed operators would have gained a safe harbor letting industry-written, FTC-approved guidelines substitute for the rules, but would otherwise have faced notice, verifiable parental consent, data-security, and parental-access requirements that constrain collecting kids' data [S2][S3]. Their interest in unrestricted data collection runs against the privacy protection the bill offered families.

The bill would have entrenched industry representatives as the authors of the compliance guidelines, with FTC approval as the only check, making self-regulation the permanent channel for children's privacy standards [S2][S3].

For adult consumers the bill only required studies, but the FTC and FCC proceedings could have laid groundwork for rules limiting the collection, reuse, disclosure, and sale of consumers' online data [S2][S3].
